## Overview

A rule says what a cell becomes; an **update scheme** says when. In SciML terms
the scheme is the algorithm passed to `solve`:

| scheme | what happens in one step | backends |
|---|---|---|
| `Synchronous()` | every cell updates at once from the previous state | all |
| `Stochastic(p)` | each cell updates with probability `p`, the rest keep their state | all |
| `Checkerboard()` | cells with even index sum update, then the odd ones | all lattice backends |
| `RandomSequential()` | cells update one at a time in a random order, in place | CPU |
| `Margolus()` | 2 × 2 blocks update together, the partition shifting each step | CPU |

Synchronous updating is the classic definition, but it is an idealisation:
real organisms do not all act at the same instant, and some patterns of
synchronous automata are artefacts of perfect synchrony.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
using Random
```

## The same rule, four schemes

The Game of Life from one random soup, under each scheme:

```{julia}
soup = Int8.(rand(Xoshiro(1), 0:1, 80, 80))
schemes = ["Synchronous" => Synchronous(), "Stochastic(0.5)" => Stochastic(0.5),
           "RandomSequential" => RandomSequential(), "Checkerboard" => Checkerboard()]
sols = [name => solve(CAProblem(Life(), soup, 200; seed=1), alg; saveat=5)
        for (name, alg) in schemes]
plot([plot(sol; c=:binary, colorbar=false, title=name, titlefontsize=10) for (name, sol) in sols]...;
     layout=(1, 4), size=(900, 250))
```

```{julia}
plt = plot(; xlabel="t", ylabel="live fraction", size=(650, 350))
for (name, sol) in sols
    plot!(plt, sol.t, [count(==(1), u) / length(u) for u in sol.u]; label=name)
end
plt
```

Synchronous Life burns down to a sparse scattering of still lifes and
oscillators, about 6% of cells alive after 200 steps. All three asynchronous
schemes instead settle quickly at a much higher, fluctuating density of around
40%: Life's characteristic structures depend on perfect synchrony, and without
it the rule behaves like a noisy, space-filling growth process.

## Synchrony artefacts: majority voting

In a majority-vote rule each cell takes the majority state of itself and its
four von Neumann neighbours. Started from a perfect checkerboard, every cell
sees four neighbours in the opposite state:

```{julia}
majority = LocalRule(VonNeumann(1)) do cell, nbrs, ctx
    cell + sum(nbrs) >= 3 ? one(cell) : zero(cell)
end
checker = Int8[isodd(i + j) for i in 1:60, j in 1:60]
changed(sol) = count(sol.u[end] .!= sol.u[end - 1])
for alg in (Synchronous(), Checkerboard(), RandomSequential())
    sol = solve(CAProblem(majority, checker, 50; seed=2), alg)
    println(rpad(nameof(typeof(alg)), 18), "cells changing in the last step: ", changed(sol))
end
```

Synchronously, every cell of the checkerboard sees four neighbours in the
opposite state and flips, so all 3600 cells change at every step, for ever: an
artefact of perfect synchrony. Under `Checkerboard` and `RandomSequential`
updating the first cells to update change the neighbourhoods of the later ones,
and the pattern freezes.

## Stochastic updating

`Stochastic(p)` is asynchrony that still runs in parallel: in each step a
random fraction `p` of cells updates. Each cell's coin is its draw number `0`,
so the run is reproducible on every backend. As `p` falls, Life's dynamics slow
and change character:

```{julia}
plt = plot(; xlabel="t", ylabel="live fraction", size=(650, 350))
for p in (1.0, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25)
    sol = solve(CAProblem(Life(), soup, 300; seed=3), Stochastic(p); saveat=5)
    plot!(plt, sol.t, [count(==(1), u) / length(u) for u in sol.u]; label="p = $p")
end
plt
```

## Block rules and the Margolus scheme

Some processes are easier to write for a block of cells than for one cell: a
particle that moves must leave one cell and enter another in the same step.
The Margolus scheme cuts the lattice into 2 × 2 blocks; a `BlockRule` maps each
block's four states, given as `(top_left, bottom_left, top_right,
bottom_right)`, to its new states, and the partition shifts by one cell
diagonally every step so that blocks overlap over time. Whatever the rule
conserves within a block, it conserves globally.

### Falling sand

Here `1` is sand, `2` is wall and `0` is empty. Within a block, sand falls into
an empty cell below it, and otherwise slides diagonally downwards if it can:

```{julia}
falling_sand = BlockRule() do block, ctx
    tl, bl, tr, br = block
    if tl == 1 && bl == 0
        tl, bl = bl, tl
    end
    if tr == 1 && br == 0
        tr, br = br, tr
    end
    if tl == 1 && br == 0 && bl != 0 && tr != 1
        tl, br = br, tl
    elseif tr == 1 && bl == 0 && br != 0 && tl != 1
        tr, bl = bl, tr
    end
    return (tl, bl, tr, br)
end

n = 64
u = zeros(Int8, n, n)
u[(end - 1):end, :] .= 2          # floor
u[40, 10:30] .= 2                 # a shelf
u[3:16, 25:40] .= 1               # a block of sand
sol = solve(CAProblem(falling_sand, u, 120), Margolus(); saveat=40)
plot([plot(sol; snapshot=i, c=[:white, :goldenrod, :grey30], colorbar=false) for i in 1:4]...;
     layout=(1, 4), size=(900, 250))
```

The amount of sand never changes:

```{julia}
[count(==(1), x) for x in sol.u]
```

### Diffusion by random rotation

Rotating each block a quarter turn clockwise or anticlockwise at random is a
lattice gas that diffuses: particles spread out but are never created or
destroyed. The coin for each block comes from its context, so the run is
reproducible.

```{julia}
rotate = BlockRule() do b, ctx
    tl, bl, tr, br = b
    bernoulli(ctx, 0.5) ? (tr, tl, br, bl) : (bl, br, tl, tr)
end
u = zeros(Int8, 96, 96)
u[40:56, 40:56] .= 1
sol = solve(CAProblem(rotate, u, 400; seed=4), Margolus(); saveat=100)
spread(x) = sqrt(sum(((Tuple(I)[1] - 48.5)^2 + (Tuple(I)[2] - 48.5)^2) * x[I]
                     for I in CartesianIndices(x)) / sum(x))
plot(plot([plot(sol; snapshot=i, c=:binary, colorbar=false) for i in (1, 3, 5)]...;
          layout=(1, 3)),
     plot(sol.t, spread.(sol.u); marker=:circle, xlabel="t", ylabel="rms distance",
          legend=false);
     layout=(1, 2), size=(900, 280))
```

```{julia}
[sum(x) for x in sol.u]
```

The particle count stays at 289 while the cloud spreads, and the mean squared
distance from the centre grows roughly linearly in time, as for diffusion.
